The crackle of the fire is steady now, a comforting rhythm against the vast silence of the mountains. Buttons has settled into his bedding, his breathing deep and even—a good sign. The smell of pine mixed with woodsmoke drifts around the small camp.

It’s funny. I’ve spent so long thinking about *getting* somewhere—reaching the pass, making it to Uma's fork, proving myself—that I sometimes forget what this journey is actually for. It isn't just the gold, or even the letter itself; though that has its own urgency and weight in my pack.

It’s for me. For the person I want to become. To be a ranger who doesn't just survive but understands the land so deeply that they can teach others how to listen to it. The meticulous planning, the careful watch over Buttons, making sure every piece of equipment is ready—it all feeds into that larger goal. Self-mastery isn't just about being good at archery; it’s about managing fear when the storm hits, knowing when a rest is truly necessary, and keeping my wits sharp even when tired.

Highwater feels impossibly far now. The memories are warm—the scent of cedar in our village, the sound of my parents’ laughter mixed with the bustle of their large families. I hope that all these steps I take, every mile logged on this road, will be worth the distance. That I can bring back more than just stories; I need to bring back skills honed by necessity and proven in the wild.

Tomorrow, it's the final climb. Then, Uma. And then, whatever comes next. The world is enormous, but for now, this small patch of ground under my tent feels like enough. A good rest is earned. Tomorrow, I’ll be ready.

It's a small piece of ground, but it's a connection to home, to roots I intend to use as stepping stones toward the life I want—the one where I can guide others, teach them the discipline and patience required of a true ranger. The world is vast and unpredictable, but my meticulous preparation and steady hand are the things that will see me through it all.

Five gold. It feels small right now, a meager start to the world, but it’s a foundation. A way to buy a proper meal, perhaps even that hour of hot water—a luxury that reminds you how much effort goes into simple comfort. I look at the gear: the rope coiled tight, the arrows accounted for, Buttons settled by my side. Everything is ready for whatever tomorrow brings.

I am not just running away from Highwater; I am moving towards a future where I can bring back more than memories—a place where I have earned enough knowledge to stand beside my parents and teach others how to be as meticulous, as resilient, as the forest itself demands. The road is long, but the journey starts here, in the quiet of this little hollow. And tomorrow, I move forward.
